samples.text:
In the past, most people worked for one company for all their life, but now many people change their job often. Some people think it is better to stay with the same employer, while others believe changing jobs brings more benefits. I will discuss both views and give my opinion.

There are several advantages of staying in one company for a long time. Firstly, employees can get job security, which means they do not need to worry about losing their income. Secondly, if a worker stay for many years, the company trust him and he can get promotion to a higher position. For example, a person who start as a junior staff can become a manager after ten years. Moreover, they can build strong relationship with their colleagues.

On the other hand, changing jobs frequently also have many benefits. When people move to a new company, they usually get a higher salary than before. They also learn new skills and experience different ways of working, which make their CV more attractive. In addition, if someone is not happy in their job, it is better to leave and find a job they enjoy instead of feeling bored for many years.

In my opinion, changing jobs is better for young people, but staying with one employer is better later in life. When people are young, they should try different jobs to find what they are good at. After that, they can stay with a good company and build their career there.

In conclusion, both staying and changing jobs have advantages. I think people should change jobs when they are young and then stay with one employer when they find the right place.

samples.text:
Attitudes to careers have changed considerably, and people now debate whether loyalty to one employer or regular job changes is the better path. While each approach has its merits, I believe that changing jobs periodically, rather than constantly, offers the greatest benefits for most people.

Remaining with the same organisation for many years can be highly rewarding. Long-serving employees develop an in-depth understanding of how their company works, which often makes them strong candidates for promotion to senior roles. They also tend to enjoy greater job security and build strong, trusting relationships with colleagues and managers. In addition, stability of this kind can make it easier to plan major life decisions, such as buying a home or starting a family.

On the other hand, people who change jobs more frequently often progress faster in terms of salary and responsibility. Moving to a new employer is frequently the quickest way to negotiate a significant pay rise, and each new role exposes the worker to different systems, technologies and working cultures. This variety helps them to develop a broad set of skills and a wider professional network, both of which is increasingly important in a fast-changing job market. Staying in one place for too long, by contrast, can lead to complacency and outdated skills.

In my opinion, the ideal lies somewhere between these extremes. Changing jobs every few months can suggest a lack of commitment, but remaining in the same position for decades may limit personal growth. Spending a few years in each role, long enough to make a real contribution, allows people to gain both depth and breadth of experience.

In conclusion, although long-term loyalty brings security and recognition, I believe that moving between employers at sensible intervals generally offers greater opportunities for development and advancement.

samples.text:
Whereas a single lifelong employer was once the norm, many workers today move between organisations several times during their careers. This has sparked debate over whether long-term loyalty or frequent change is more advantageous. Having considered both sides, I would argue that the answer depends partly on career stage, but that a willingness to move is generally more beneficial.

There is much to be said for staying with one employer. Over time, an employee accumulates detailed knowledge of the organisation's systems, clients and culture, which can make them indispensable and position them well for internal promotion. Long tenure also tends to bring stability, both financial and emotional, together with close working relationships that can make the workplace more fulfilling. Employers, for their part, often reward such commitment with additional benefits and greater trust.

Nevertheless, frequent job changes carry advantages that are difficult to ignore. Moving to a new organisation is often the most effective way to secure a substantial increase in salary, since external candidates can negotiate from a stronger position than existing staff. Each move also exposes the employee to unfamiliar challenges, methods and colleagues, accelerating the acquisition of skills and broadening their professional network. In a labour market where entire industries can be transformed within a decade, such adaptability is arguably a greater form of security than loyalty to a single firm.

On balance, I believe that moving between employers is more beneficial, particularly in the early and middle stages of a career, when breadth of experience matters most. That said, changing jobs too often can undermine credibility and prevent people from seeing projects through to completion. The most rewarding pattern is perhaps to stay long enough in each role to achieve something meaningful before moving on.

In conclusion, while long service offers stability and recognition, periodic job changes generally provide faster growth, higher earnings and greater resilience in an uncertain economy.
samples.why: Both views thoroughly explored with extended support · clear, qualified opinion · logical progression and well-managed paragraphs · precise, natural vocabulary (long tenure, indispensable) · wide range of complex structures without errors.
